description: Durand White Oak observed in Cameron Park, near the Clubhouse, on a bluff high above the Brazos River valley at Waco TX. That tree is gone as of Dec-2018. Still another Durand Oak is found nearby right next to the Clubhouse. A Durand Oak prior champ (from Jun-1969) was also found in the Big Tree Registry about a quarter-mile southeast (near Proctor Springs), but that tree appears to have also died and was recently cut down; the two right-most photos show the reported location. Also at Proctor Springs, I observed two super large oaks (which appear to be White Oak, based on the leaves on the ground) and a modestly large Bur Oak, along with what I took to be several specimens of Durand Oak.  Obviously, Durand Oak is not uncommon in this area, although iNat users have not documented any others in the Brazos valley to date.

description:
Stephen F. Austin Death Site Oak(s) just north of West Columbia TX on south side of Oilfield Rd.  This location is where the "Father Of Texas" died in 1836 unexpectedly at a young age at the home of George B. McKinstry, once present on this site. Four large Live Oaks occupy the privately-held property today, with three of these very near the public road.  The property was purchased in 1994, restored from being an old oilfield junkyard, and is maintained by Mr. Billy F. Price. It is open to the public through an unlocked gate.  The largest oak is the one by the historical marker; its trunk circumference (breast height) was measured as 159”. The fourth oak is at the south side of the property, near what appears to be a field nursery for young oak trees.  The age of the trees has been estimated, indicating that they were present in 1836. Mr. Price has pioneered a project to grow trees from acorns collected under these trees; a sapling planted at every school in Texas named after Stephen F. Austin, and also on the grounds of each of the state's 254 county courthouses (now complete), as well as at the George Bush museum and grave in Brazos Co.  The Daughters Of The Republic Of Texas hold a commemorative flag-raising ceremony every Nov. 3rd (Austin's birthday) at the site.
More info: https://texasbob.com/travel/tbt_sfaustin.html

description:
Declared Texas State Champion Live Oak on 25-Apr-2024!

Live Oak observed along south side of North Road, between Lake Jackson and Brazoria TX.  This tree was measured in 1999-2000 and was declared the largest Live Oak in Brazoria County in a project at that time by the county chapter of Texas Master Gardeners. At that time, the dimensions were 318" trunk circumference, 80' height and 94.3' crown spread (Tree Index of 422).  The county title passed to the San Bernard Oak in 2003, which also was recognized as the Texas state champ in 2003-2016.  The tree pictured above was re-measured on 12-Feb-2019 by a team from the Cradle Of Texas chapter of Texas Master Naturalists, with new dimensions of 349" trunk circumference (at 4.5' above ground surface), 77' height and 76' crown spread (Tree Index of 445). Given that the then-current Texas state champ had a Tree Index of 427, it seemed likely that this tree could become a new state champ. At that time, this tree was not found in the Texas Big Tree Registry, so it was assumed that it had never been previously nominated at the state level, so it was nominated on 4-Apr-2022, and re-submitted on 7-Jan-2023. Word was received on 4-May-2024 that it had been re-measured by the Texas Forest Service in Jun-2023, and officially declared the new champ on 25-Apr-2024. Brazoria County reclaims the title!

The right-most three photos are from the 1960's, indicating the tree was a local favorite even then.

description:
I have visited this population before in fruiting season  (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/7736433). 
 This observation is to document several points:
1) There are some new stems coming up (1st 3 photos) but most stems bear leaves that overwintered.  No indication of fall deciduousness.  
2) New leaves have a very close downy surface (photo 3); some old leaves are glabrous underneath (and green), others have some down (and are pale).  Upper surface shiny, leathery. 
4) Some leaves have red midribs. 
5) All have very short petioles (~sessile).  All are bristle-tipped. 
6) I saw no lobed leaves.
7) Population very low stature (<1 m, no trunklike stems, plants form a ground cover and may be joined underground).  
8) Buds are small. Twigs are pubescent.
Overall the leaves are very similar to oak I'm trying to ID at https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/21270437 (except for lacking lobes), but the buds are smaller and the habit is distinctly different, as those stems are upright, trunklike and taller, and the twigs are glabrous.  EDIT: those seem to have turned out to be bluejack oak, Quercus incana.

The large tree was moved in 2012 from a location 1500 feet north of here when local roads were widened. description:
Bastard Oak observed in Austin TX.  It is believed this tree is the one that has been certified by the Texas Forest Service as the state champion for Bigelow Oak (Quercus sinuata var. breviloba), and is located on private property (location is not reported at the Texas Big Tree Registry website, and so has been obscured here). It is so great that the owners have preserved the tree in its urban setting!  Dimensions are reported to be 46' height, 124" trunk circumference, and 78' crown spread for a Tree Index of 189.  These dimensions are roughly equivalent to those of the two certified state co-champ Durand White Oak (Quercus sinuata var. sinuata) specimens (with Tree Indexes of 221 and 223), one of which is located in the same county:
https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/19159542

Interestingly, this specimen seems to comply to a degree with the description for Quercus sinuata var. sinuata, as summarized in the key in Efloras.org for the species:
Trees to 20 m, trunk usually solitary; moist bottomlands and riparian habitats.	------>var. sinuata
Shrubs or small trees to 3(–5) m, often forming thickets, trunks multiple from near ground; dry limestone hills. ---->var. breviloba
Thus, it remains open to discussion whether this is var. breviloba or var. sinuata, or perhaps (even probably) some intergrade.

description:
This is a small, isolated, but apparently naturally occurring stand of Oregon White Oak located in a residential neighborhood along SE Lake Rd in Bellevue, sandwiched between I-90 and the shore of Lake Washington, just east of Enatai Beach Park. I am not aware of any other native populations of Oregon White Oak in Bellevue.

The stand is considerably reduced in extent since I first visited it in August 1984; at that time I noted that the stand occupied about 5 acres, but much of the area has been cleared since then. Also in 1984 I noted that there was one obvious pre-settlement tree, an Oregon white oak that about 75 ft. tall and about 6 ft. dbh. When I returned to the site a few years later this tree had been removed. All of the remaining trees (including those still present) appeared to be less than 150 years old.

It has been hypothesized that isolated Oregon white oak sites in western Washington are often associated with locations of Native American activity. According to Waterman's 1922 paper, this site is documented as having been called "TL!utsa"lus" by the native people who lived in the area. This was translated to the phrase "tying a mesh". There was also a village site located nearby at the head of Mercer Slough.

description: This is, to my knowledge, the very northern-most natural occurrence of California Black Oak. At least, the species has never been reported to be growing naturally from north of Lane County, and this site is only about 4 miles south of the county line. The black oaks grow in a mixed population with Oregon white oak, as well as lesser amounts of bigleaf maple and Douglas-fir. Most of the black oaks at this site are in younger age classes, so recruitment seems to be occurring without difficulty. There is no obvious explanation for why black oak does not occur farther north, there are no obvious ecological, topographic, or climatic factors that would explain this circumstance.

description:
Valley Oak (Quercus lobata)

June 11, 2019
William B. Ide Adobe State Historic Park
Red Bluff, Tehama County, California

Valley Oak is an entirely endemic oak species to California and it grows heaviest in the northern and central parts of the state but extends its growth into southern California. The specimen from which we took these images was growing next to the Sacramento River in what is according to the iNat range map its most extensive area of growth. Valley Oak then is a native species to North America and to California specifically. See the range map here: https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/49011-Quercus-lobata

10 species of Oaks have been identified growing in Tehama County, California, according to the iNat archive. A careful comparison of the leaves of the oak we observed growing at the state park with those of all 10 species easily leads to the conclusion that ours is Valley Oak. The 10 oak species may be viewed here: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations?place_id=1530&subview=table&taxon_id=47851&view=species

description: The main purpose of this hike was to survey the PCT between Wellman trail junction and Deer Springs Trail junction. This is another stunted canyon oak at high elevation

This White Oak grows behind the wood shed at the Macoskey Center in Slippery Rock PA. You can distinctly tell this is a white oak based on its deeply lobed, smooth leaves. White Oak typically live in moist, well-drained uplands and lowlands.

This Tree wasn't fruited with many acorns yet, but we did find a couple on the ground. As you can see from the photograph, we found a baby white oak acorn on the ground. The acorns range from .4 inches long to 1.3 inches long enclosed by a shallow cup. 

White Oak have widespread branches and a rounded crown. They usually grow up to 80-100 feet and have a hearty diameter of 3-4 feet. The leaves are 4-9 inches long and 2-4 inches wide. 

Growing around and under the tree are various types of other trees and weeds. Growing to the right of the oak is a Norway Spruce(Picea abies). Underneath the oak are some Rasberry bushes (Rubus idaeus). There are also goldenrod(Solidago sp.) Blooming to the left of the tree. Since the White oak is growing behind and wood shed, it was hard to access the base and see what bugs and other life were growing there. I can imagine there are ants and spiders.  
Birds that frequent that Oak tree are Blue Jays (Cyanocitta cristata), Northern Cardinal (Cardinalis cardinalis), Pileated Woodpecker (Dryocopus pileatus). There are many birdfeeders around the area of the White oak that attract these birds.


The high temperature for the day was. 86 degrees Fahrenheit. The low was 56 degrees Fahrenheit. It was a beautiful sunny day with winds blowing SW at 2mph.

description:
This oak was spotted in a wooded lot near homes. It is a relatively dry area with more sand than dirt. The bark was a brownish grey color and deeply furrowed. The tree had pubescent twigs growing that were chestnut in color. The leaves were about 15 cm in length and about 8cm wide. I was able to distinguish this oak as the Quercus laevis because of the tapered leaf base and the overall “turkey’s foot” shape, which differs from the Southern Red Oak’s u-shaped base leaves. The tree also had acorns present higher up in the branches, so I was not able to distinguish color. 

“This species is similar to Q. falcata in leaf shape and can be distinguished by the tapered leaf base and axillary tufts, whereas the southern red oak leaves have a u-shaped base and pubescence covering the entire lower leaf surface.”- https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=QULA2

description:
A Valley Oak (Quercus lobata), photographed at Tree Life Cycles Park in east San Jose, CA.  Note that there are 9 photos in the set of pictures dpcumenting this tree:

Shot 1:  Distant shot of the tree, showing its height and breadth, as well as its general form.  Note the robustness of this tree's trunk and major boughs.

Shot 2:  A closeup of the bark covering this Valley Oak's trunk.  Note its rough, rugged, heavily creviced appearance and light gray color.

Shot 3:  A shot of this Valley Oak's canopy.  Note the robustness of its boughs and relative openness of its canopy.

Shot 4:  A shot of one of the leaves of this Valley Oak.

Shot 5:  A shot of more of this Valley Oak's leaves.  Some of the leaves in Shots 4 and 5 are broader or more irregularly shaped than is typical for a Valley Oak, so there may be some hybridization going on with it.

Shot 6 shows the gall of a Spined Turban Gall Wasp (Andricus douglasii), found growing on one of this Valley Oak's leaves.

Shot 7 shows the gall of a California Gall Wasp (Andricus quercuscalifornicus), found growing on one of this Valley Oak's branches.

Shot 8 shows the gall of a couple of Round Gall Wasp (Besbicus conspicuus), found growing on another of this Valley Oak's leaves.

Shot 9 shows the gall of a Convoluted Gall Wasp (Andricus confertus), found growing on another of this Valley Oak's leaves.

Along a mesic river bluff

This seems to be the hybrid between Q. rubra and Q. velutina. Keyed out using Flora of the Chicago Region

The distal scales of the winter buds are distinctly pubescent, unlike Q. rubra which has glabrous buds. The buds are also slightly angled. Q. velutina has angular buds that are entirely densely pubescent. I unfortunately neglected to take a good photo, but the second picture does show an abaxial leaf surface, in the background, with obvious tufts of hairs in the axils like in Q. velutina. The acorns caps are turbinate like Q. velutina, but with appressed scales like Q. rubra.

If Q. velutina is currently present on the site, or on the North Branch of the Chicago River for that matter, it is very rare and I have yet to find it. But Q. rubra is of course very abundant. 

Perhaps Q. velutina was once more abundant, and as its populations waned it became more likely that its pollen would pollinate a separate species. Or perhaps a chance dispersal brought a lone Q. velutina to the area, and it crossed with the only other receptive mates in the areas. Another possible Q. velutina hybrid was also found nearby:

description:
Along a mesic river bluff

This seems to be the hybrid between Q. ellipsoidalis and Q. velutina. Keyed out using Flora of the Chicago Region

The distal scales of the winter buds are densely pubescent, and the proximal scales are sparsely pubescent or at least ciliate. Q. velutina has buds that are densely pubescent throughout. The axils of the vein on the undersides of the leaves are sparsely pubescent. Q. velutina and Q. x vaga, the hybrid of Q. velutina and Q. palustris, are noted as having denser tufts of hairs in the leaf axils. Q. x vaga is also noted as having buds up to 6mm. The buds here look to be longer than that.

If Q. velutina is currently present on the site, or on the North Branch of the Chicago River for that matter, it is very rare and I have yet to find it. In this particular area, Q. ellipsoidalis is present but uncommon, while it can be rather common just a few miles upstream of here. On the lower part of the North Branch, Q. ellipsoidalis tends to be restricted to mesic edges of bluffs on the southern and western banks of the river. 

Perhaps Q. velutina was once more abundant, and as its populations waned it became more likely that its pollen would pollinate a separate species. Or perhaps a chance dispersal brought a lone Q. velutina to the area, and it crossed with the only other receptive mates in the areas. Another possible Q. velutina hybrid was also found nearby:

Rare shrub (only one seen) growing in deep, dry, white sand with Aristida stricta, Bulbostylis ciliatifolia var. coarctata, Cnidoscolus stimulosus, Euphorbia ipecacuanhae, Pinus palustris, Quercus geminata, Q. hemisphaerica, Q. laevis, Rhynchospora megalocarpa, Schizachyrium scoparium, and other sand hill stuff.  Quercus margarettae grows nearby in the preserve.

Unfortunately I missed the only acorn it had by just a few days.

Q. × harbisonii and Q. geminata are compared in the last photo.

Thanks to Keith Bradley ( @linaceae ) for encouraging me to visit this little tree.
